summary:
FIREMAP Fusion : Bringing MODIS and VIIRS Fire Data Together

I developed FIREMAP Fusion to make it easier to explore and compare active fire data collected by NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites. The idea came from the challenge of working with observations from different satellite sensors and understanding how their fire detections relate to one another.

Using Python and Streamlit, I built an interactive application that collects NASA FIRMS fire detection data and brings the observations into a common format. Users can explore fire locations on a map, view detection activity, compare MODIS and VIIRS records, and examine where both sensors detected activity within the same grid cell and day.

Through this project, I wanted to show how combining satellite observations can provide a clearer picture of fire activity. I also learned that different sensors have different capabilities, so their results need to be interpreted carefully. I hope FIREMAP Fusion can make satellite fire data more accessible and useful for people interested in environmental monitoring.
details:
Project Overview

FIREMAP Fusion is an interactive web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge of Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. The idea behind this project is to make satellite-based fire observations easier to explore and compare by bringing data from different satellite sensors into one platform.

MODIS and VIIRS provide valuable information about active fires, but their observations differ in spatial resolution, sensor characteristics and detection capabilities. This makes direct comparisons challenging. FIREMAP Fusion aims to address this by organizing their observations into a common data structure while preserving the original sensor information.

Interactive Satellite Hotspot Mapping

The first feature of FIREMAP Fusion is its interactive hotspot map, which displays active-fire observations geographically. The application uses different marker colours to distinguish MODIS and VIIRS records, allowing users to explore where detections occur and how observations from different sensors are distributed across the study area.

Figure 1 : Interactive Active-Fire Detection Map

Figure 1. FIREMAP Fusion interactive map showing MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections across the study region in Sabah, Malaysia. Orange markers represent MODIS observations, while blue markers represent VIIRS observations. The map allows users to explore the geographical distribution of satellite detection records.

Harmonized Data Processing and Methodology

FIREMAP Fusion uses NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) as its primary data source. The application retrieves recent observations through the NASA FIRMS Area API and also supports uploading FIRMS CSV datasets.

The downloaded records are processed using Python and Pandas into a common data structure. Important fields include latitude, longitude, acquisition date and time, sensor identity, confidence information and Fire Radiative Power (FRP), where available. This approach allows records from different satellite products to be examined together without removing their original source information.

Figure 2 : Harmonized Data Structure and Source Information

Figure 2. Data quality and harmonization interface displaying the number of records received from each source product and a preview of the common observation structure. The initial dataset contains 22 records, consisting of 2 MODIS observations and 20 VIIRS observations. This demonstrates how the application organizes different satellite records into a consistent format while retaining their sensor identities.

Cross-Sensor Comparison and Initial Findings

One of the main functions of FIREMAP Fusion is comparing observations from MODIS and VIIRS. To demonstrate this, the application groups observations according to a common spatial grid and acquisition date. This provides a simple way to examine whether detections from both sensors occur within the same grid cell on the same day.

For the initial Sabah dataset, the application used a 0.01-degree comparison grid. The comparison identified one grid cell/day represented by both sensors, one represented by MODIS only and nine represented by VIIRS only. This produced a same-cell/day overlap of 9.1% among the occupied grid cells.

Figure 3 : MODIS and VIIRS Cross-Sensor Comparison

Figure 3. Cross-sensor comparison dashboard showing the raw number of detections from MODIS and VIIRS and their same-cell/day comparison. The initial dataset contains 2 MODIS records and 20 VIIRS records, with a calculated overlap of 9.1% using the selected spatial grid and matching method.

This result is an initial demonstration of the comparison method, not a measurement of satellite accuracy or proof that the sensors detected different physical fires. The overlap is sensitive to grid size, acquisition timing, sensor resolution and geographical differences. Further testing with larger historical datasets and more advanced matching methods would be necessary for stronger conclusions.

Active-Fire Detection Activity Visualization

The application also provides a detection activity chart that helps users examine the available observations over time. By separating MODIS and VIIRS records, users can see how the detection records are distributed across the available observation period.

Figure 4 : Active-Fire Detection Activity

Figure 4. Monthly detection activity visualization showing the distribution of available MODIS and VIIRS records. This feature provides an overview of the observations within the selected dataset. Since the current demonstration uses a limited recent data period, it should not be interpreted as a long-term seasonal or historical fire trend.

Technology and Development

FIREMAP Fusion was developed using Python and Streamlit to create an interactive web application. Pandas was used for data processing, Folium for geographical mapping, Plotly for data visualization and Requests for communicating with the NASA FIRMS API. The development process focused on creating a platform that is accessible, understandable and useful for exploring satellite observations. Users can retrieve recent NASA FIRMS data, visualize detection locations, compare sensor records, inspect the harmonized data table and download the processed observations as a CSV file.

Benefits, Innovation and Future Impact

The main contribution of FIREMAP Fusion is providing a single interactive environment for exploring and comparing active-fire observations from different satellite sensors. Instead of manually examining separate datasets, users can view the records together, explore their geographical distribution and investigate where observations overlap.

The application could benefit students, researchers, environmental observers and people interested in satellite-based fire monitoring. Future development could include longer historical datasets, improved spatial and temporal matching, additional satellite products, validation against independent fire information and more advanced analysis of fire activity.

FIREMAP Fusion is currently a working prototype. It does not claim to predict fires, calculate burned area or provide a calibrated measurement of fire intensity. Its purpose is to make multi-sensor active-fire observations easier to explore, understand and compare through a transparent and accessible approach.
